title: Out-of-control Hamiltonian Learning
authors: Weiyuan Gong, Muzhou Ma, Sitan Chen, Jordan Cotler, Hsin-Yuan Huang
abstract: Learning the Hamiltonian of a many-body system from its dynamics is a central task in quantum science, yet the algorithms with the strongest provable guarantees assume some level of quantum control--fast, arbitrary single-qubit gates interleaved with time evolution, and measurements in arbitrary bases--that is beyond the capabilities of near-term analog quantum simulators. Motivated by analog atom- and ion-based platforms, we study Hamiltonian learning under minimal access models.   Uniform state preparation and measurements: We first consider the setting where in every experiment, one can rotate each qubit to the same state, perform short-time evolution, and measure every qubit in the same basis. Surprisingly, we show that for generic 2-local Hamiltonians on any interaction graph, all of the parameters can be reconstructed from such experiments.   Computational basis state preparation and measurements: We then consider a similarly constrained setting, but where state preparation and measurement are restricted to the computational basis. For nearest-neighbor Hamiltonians with only Pauli $X/Z$ interactions, a class which captures contemporary Rydberg atom platforms, we show that over 1D and 2D rectangular lattices, all of the parameters can be reconstructed from such experiments up to unavoidable gauges.   Our protocols introduce new techniques for solving structured polynomial systems over an extensive number of parameters. Taken together, our results suggest that one can learn a great deal from the dynamics of quantum many-body systems even under the most stringent experimental constraints.
summary: This paper tackles the challenge of determining a quantum system's Hamiltonian using only limited experimental measurements, mimicking real-world analog quantum simulators. It proves that even with severe constraints on state preparation and measurement, the Hamiltonian parameters can be robustly recovered. This work provides crucial theoretical guarantees for the characterization of complex quantum many-body physics.
main_problem: The central task is learning the unknown Hamiltonian of a many-body quantum system solely from measurements of its time evolution dynamics.
main_result: The authors prove that even under highly restricted experimental access models (like uniform or Z-basis measurements), the Hamiltonian parameters can be fully reconstructed for generic 2-local Hamiltonians.
method: The problem is mathematically reduced to solving highly structured systems of polynomial equations derived from short-time evolution probabilities, utilizing advanced algebraic techniques and numerical refinement methods.
model_or_system: The focus is on 2-local Hamiltonians on arbitrary interaction graphs, motivated by programmable analog quantum simulators such as Rydberg atom and trapped-ion platforms.
key_observables: Transition probabilities $p^{\hat{a}, \hat{b}}_{z	o z'}(t)$ measured from short-time evolution, which encode the Hamiltonian parameters.
important_parameters: The reconstruction is shown to be possible for generic Hamiltonians, with complexity scaling related to $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ in the time required for measurements.
main_assumptions: The results rely on the Hamiltonian being 'generic' (coefficients perturbed by small noise) and the ability to perform measurements under specific, constrained access models.
figures_summary: Figure 1 and Table 1 summarize the learnability results based on the specific access model (Uniform vs. Z-basis) and the type of Hamiltonian considered.
paper_structure: The paper is structured by analyzing different access models: first, the uniform control model, showing full parameter recovery; second, the Z-basis access model, showing recovery for specific lattice Hamiltonians up to unavoidable gauges.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the feasibility of characterizing complex, interacting quantum systems using near-term, resource-constrained quantum hardware, which is a major bottleneck in quantum simulation.
